newsitem.title: UK: Annan, in London, faces calls for UN reform.
newsitem.headline: Annan, in London, faces calls for UN reform.

text.p: United Nations Secretary General Kofi Annan flew to Britain on Tuesday for a three-day visit and was expected to face calls for reform of the world body and its high-spending specialised agencies.
Following the appointment of Annan at the end of last year, British officials believe prospects for financial reforms at the United Nations look more promising than they have done for some time.

Annan will meet Queen Elizabeth, Prime Minister John Major, Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind and Tony Blair, leader of the main opposition Labour Party, which is favourite to win Britain's upcoming election.
Annan will meet Israeli President Ezer Weizman, who is also on a visit to London.

With the queen, the two will on Wednesday attend the unveiling of a monument to Swedish diplomat Raoul Wallenberg, who disappeared after helping thousands of Jews escape from the Nazis in Hungary during World War Two. Wallenberg was an uncle of Annan's wife Nane.

Annan's talks with British leaders are expected to cover the broad issue of reform of the United Nations and Britain hopes he will endorse a "root and branch" review of the U.N.'s specialised agencies.
Agencies such as the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees acount for about two-thirds of the $7.5 billion that the United Nations spends every year.
Officials acknowledge that it will be difficult for Annan to rein in the agencies because they operate at arm's length from the U.N. itself.

Britain believes that the appointment of Madeleine Albright as U.S. Secretary of State and the fact that Annan has forged better relations with Congress suggest there will be progress on the payment of overdue U.S. contributions to the United Nations.
Britain also wants to see progress on the issue of how much the U.S. should contribute to the United Nations' general and peacekeeping budgets.

Annan's talks in London are also expected to cover reform and enlargement of the 15-member Security Council. Britain wants to see Germany and Japan accepted as permanent members and overall enlargement of the council to a maximum of 20 or 21.
Annan, a career U.N. official, is thought to enjoy the confidence of his U.N. colleagues as he prepares to reform the world body.
